A major new report from the Hudson Institute warns that legacy tankers like the KC-135 and KC-46—essentially modified commercial airliners with giant radar cross-sections—are sitting ducks for China's ultra-long-range "tanker-killer" air-to-air missiles like the PL-17 (Breaking Defense).

Developed under the RACER program to tackle the deadly "last tactical mile" on future battlefields, the robotic vehicles used satellite feeds and sensor suites to navigate obstacles, spot targets, call up unmanned wingmen, and cue precision rocket strikes.

He spent his final days bringing his surrounded soldiers home. Sixty-two years later, his country finally brought him home. 🇺🇸

In November 1950, Lieutenant Colonel Don Carlos Faith Jr. commanded the 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, near the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea. Chinese forces had encircled the Americans in brutal winter cold — temperatures plunging, weapons jamming in the freeze, wounded men fighting simply to survive.

Faith refused to stay behind the lines. Again and again he exposed himself to enemy fire, directing his men and personally leading counterattacks. When his battered force linked up with another surrounded American unit, he took command of the combined group — the force history remembers as Task Force Faith — and led the desperate fight to break out toward friendly lines, roadblock after roadblock standing in the way.

On December 1, Faith led the assault on an enemy roadblock himself, advancing with his pistol and throwing grenades. Shrapnel tore into him, but he kept directing his men until the obstacle fell. He succumbed to his wounds the following day. In the chaos of the retreat, his body could not be recovered.

He was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor in 1951. His wife and his four-year-old daughter, Bobbie, accepted the decoration — with no grave to visit. In 2012, after decades of uncertainty, military specialists identified his remains through forensic evidence and DNA. On April 17, 2013, Don Faith was laid to rest with full military honors at Arlington National Cemetery. His daughter was there. He had spent his last days fighting to bring his soldiers home — and more than six decades later, his country finally brought him home.

She was 21, with a wedding to plan and a lifetime ahead of her. Instead, her family met her at Arlington. 🇺🇸

Sergeant Ashly Lynn Moyer grew up in Pennsylvania, graduated from Emmaus High School in 2003, and joined the Army with her whole future in front of her. Assigned to the 630th Military Police Company, she deployed to Iraq — and dreamed, like so many young soldiers, of the life waiting after the deployment: marriage, a family, coming home.

On March 3, 2007, Moyer was driving in a military convoy through Baghdad when an improvised explosive device struck her armored vehicle. She lost her life alongside two soldiers she served with, Sergeant Michael C. Peek, 23, and Sergeant Brandon A. Parr, 25 — three young lives, gone in a single blast.

Her boyfriend, fellow soldier Jake Wells, was there that day. He had planned to propose when they returned to the United States that summer. When the explosion set her vehicle ablaze, Wells ran toward the flames to reach her — but the fire and the ammunition cooking off inside kept him from getting to her. It is the kind of loss that follows a person forever.

On March 16, 2007, her family and friends laid her to rest at Arlington National Cemetery. In 2012, an Army Reserve Center in Pennsylvania was dedicated in her honor. Ashly Moyer deserves to be remembered not only for how she served, but for the future she never got to live — a daughter, a loved one, a young woman with everything still ahead of her.

FROM THE ROOFTOPS OF MARJAH TO THE VIRTUAL BATTLEFIELD: MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT KYLE CARPENTER JOINS MODERN WARFARE 4

Medal of Honor recipient and retired U.S. Marine Corps Corporal Kyle Carpenter has been immortalized as a playable operator in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone, arriving as part of the charity-driven C.O.D.E. Valor Pack.

Known worldwide for his supreme sacrifice in Marjah, Afghanistan, on November 21, 2010—where he deliberately threw his body over an enemy grenade to shield his fellow Marine—Carpenter's inclusion brings real-world legacy directly into the tactical shooter franchise.

 Rather than just lending his likeness, Carpenter worked closely with the development team on the Valor Pack, featuring operator skins modeled from his deployment, an M4 weapon blueprint, custom patches, and a personalized combat knife engraved with his name and rank.

Supporting a Vital Mission: One hundred percent of Activision's net proceeds from the C.O.D.E. Valor Pack go directly to the Call of Duty Endowment, funding programs that help military veterans transition into high-quality civilian careers after leaving active duty.

In the Hanoi Hilton, the guards answered to their commanders. The prisoners answered to James Stockdale. 🇺🇸

When Commander James Stockdale's A-4 Skyhawk was shot down over North Vietnam on September 9, 1965, he became the highest-ranking American naval officer in captivity — and the leader of the prisoner resistance. From inside Hoa Lo Prison, Stockdale built an organization out of whispers and wall-taps: a code of conduct for men under torture, secret communications between cells, and one unbreakable rule — nobody cooperates, nobody bows, everybody comes home with honor.

The North Vietnamese isolated him for it: years in solitary, long stretches in leg irons in the punishment annex the POWs called Alcatraz. In 1969, chosen to be paraded in a propaganda film, Stockdale beat his own face with a stool and cut himself with a razor fragment rather than be used — he would be photographed battered or not at all. His captors understood the message: this man would die before he bent. In the aftermath, the worst of the torture campaign eased.

Stockdale came home in February 1973, pictured here descending from the aircraft a free man, and received the Medal of Honor in 1976. Eight years a prisoner, four of them in solitary — and the men he led credit his iron example with bringing them home alive, together, and unashamed. He died in 2005, an admiral, a philosopher of endurance, and the standard by which American POWs are still measured.

They put him on television to lie for them. Instead, blinking slowly, he told the whole world the truth. 🇺🇸

Commander Jeremiah Denton, a Navy A-6 Intruder pilot, was shot down over North Vietnam on July 18, 1965, and dragged into the prison system the Americans called the Hanoi Hilton. In May 1966, his captors sat him before Japanese television cameras for a propaganda interview, expecting a broken man to parrot their script.

Denton gave them the performance they wanted with his voice — while his eyes told a different story. As he spoke, he blinked, again and again, in Morse code: T-O-R-T-U-R-E. American intelligence officers studying the film caught it — the first proof the world had that American POWs were being tortured. It is one of the most extraordinary acts of defiance ever committed in front of an enemy's own camera.

Denton endured seven years and seven months of captivity, much of it in solitary and in the punishment camp the prisoners called Alcatraz, and came home in February 1973 — the first man off the plane at Clark Air Base, where he spoke for all of them: "We are honored to have had the opportunity to serve our country under difficult circumstances." He retired a Rear Admiral, served Alabama in the United States Senate, and died in 2014. The blink that outsmarted an empire still teaches every American service member what resistance means.

The United States government and NATO have officially selected Poland to host Europe’s dedicated regional maintenance and servicing facility for Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) interceptor missiles, beating out rival proposals from Germany, the Netherlands, and Norway.

 Announced during NATO’s Conference of National Armaments Directors, placing the €227 million sustainment center in Poland directly anchors the alliance's most vital air and ballistic missile defense logistics hub within immediate proximity to the eastern theater.

With PAC-3 interceptors in extreme demand across NATO inventories and Ukrainian frontline defense networks, the facility is designed to dramatically slash transit turnaround times—keeping launchers loaded and interceptors operational without having to ship munitions across the Atlantic to the United States.

 While Poland will host the primary maintenance infrastructure, the project leverages broad multinational backing, integrating critical supply chain nodes led by key European partners including Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden alongside Lockheed Martin.

Starved to 98 pounds in a jungle prison, he crawled out of it — and then outran the jungle itself. 🇺🇸

Dieter Dengler grew up in the ruins of postwar Germany dreaming of American airplanes, crossed the ocean as a teenager, and earned his wings as a U.S. Navy pilot. On February 1, 1966, flying an A-1 Skyraider from the carrier Ranger on a secret mission over Laos, his plane was hit and crashed in the jungle. Dengler survived the crash — and walked straight into a Pathet Lao patrol.

What followed was months of torture: hung upside down, beaten, dragged, starved, staked to the ground in the camp as the prisoners wasted away. On June 29, 1966, the starving prisoners made their break. Dengler got out — one of only two of the escapees to survive the jungle — and then did the hardest part alone: 23 days evading recapture on foot, barefoot, eating what the wild offered, hiding from the men hunting him.

On July 20, 1966, an American Skyraider pilot spotted a signal on the jungle floor — a parachute laid out as an SOS by a man who refused to die — and helicopters pulled Dieter Dengler out, weighing less than 100 pounds, smiling for the cameras days later. He received the Navy Cross, flew again, and remains the only American airman to escape a Laotian prison camp and live to tell it.

He bombed Japan, rotted in its allies' cells for 40 months — then went back to Japan to love its people. 🇺🇸

Corporal Jacob DeShazer was the bombardier on the last plane of the Doolittle Raid, the daring carrier-launched strike on Tokyo of April 18, 1942. Out of fuel over occupied China, his crew bailed out into the night — straight into Japanese hands. Eight Raiders were captured; three were executed, one starved to death. DeShazer endured forty months of cells, hunger, disease and beatings, most of it in solitary confinement, not knowing if he would ever see Oregon again.

In that darkness, a smuggled Bible reached his cell — and DeShazer made a vow that sounds impossible: if he lived, he would return to Japan not with hatred, but as a missionary. He lived. Freed in August 1945, he kept the vow: in 1948 Jacob DeShazer went back to Japan and spent thirty years preaching to the people who had caged him.

A pamphlet telling his story fell into the hands of Mitsuo Fuchida — the commander who led the attack on Pearl Harbor. It helped change Fuchida's life; the two former enemies met, shook hands, and became friends. Jacob DeShazer died in 2008 at 95 — a POW who answered torture with the most disarming weapon ever carried into a prison camp: forgiveness.

In a historic ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit struck down core provisions of the 1958 Federal Switchblade Act, holding that automatically opening knives qualify as protected "Arms" under the plain text of the Second Amendment.

Dismantling a 1950s Ban: Enacted in 1958 amid 1950s pop-culture panics over juvenile delinquency, Section 1242 of the Federal Switchblade Act made it a federal crime to manufacture, transport, or sell automatic knives across state lines. The appellate panel found that the federal government failed to demonstrate any historical tradition justifying an interstate commercial ban.

Knives Are Constitutionally Protected "Arms": Applying the Supreme Court's historical-tradition framework, Chief Judge Jennifer Walker Elrod wrote for the panel that bladed tools have been used for self-defense throughout American history. The court explicitly held that the right to keep and bear arms necessarily includes the right to manufacture, ship, and acquire them through interstate commerce.

What Changes (and What Doesn't): While the decision represents a major victory for pro-knife advocacy groups like Knife Rights and clears federal interstate trade barriers within the circuit, it does not automatically override individual state or municipal concealed-carry and blade-length statutes, which remain governed under separate local laws.

They called him unbroken — and after 47 days at sea and two years in the camps, the name fit. 🇺🇸

Louis Zamperini was an Olympic runner from California who raced at the 1936 Berlin Games, and when war came he became a bombardier on a B-24 over the Pacific. On May 27, 1943, his crippled bomber, the Green Hornet, fell into the ocean during a rescue search. Zamperini and two crewmates survived on a tiny raft — drinking rain, catching fish and birds, fending off sharks — for 47 days, among the longest sea survivals in history. One of the three died on the raft. The other two washed up alive — straight into Japanese hands.

What followed was worse than the ocean: more than two years in prisoner-of-war camps, singled out for torment by a sadistic guard the prisoners called "the Bird," who beat the famous Olympian with a belt, starved him, and tried to break the thing in him that would not bend. It never broke. Zamperini came home in 1945 carrying nightmares that nearly destroyed him with drink — until, by his own account, faith put him back together, and the man who had every reason to hate flew back to Japan to forgive his captors face to face.

He died in 2014 at 97, a torch-bearer, a mentor to generations of young men, and the subject of the book and film "Unbroken." The title is not poetry. It is a description.

Lance Corporal Joshua Moore occupied a hide near Marjah, Afghanistan, with several other scout snipers when their position came under attack. Two Marines right outside the structure fell wounded. Suddenly, Moore felt something bounce off his back. He turned and found two enemy grenades on the floor. Without hesitation, Moore picked up one and threw it out the door, where the grenade safely exploded away from the Marines. As he grabbed the second grenade to throw back, he realized it was corroded and defective. Moore then ran outside into the enemy fire to help the wounded. Using his M4 and grenade launcher, Moore neutralized the enemy position 100 meters away while others moved the casualties to safety. Moore then helped clear a LZ for medevac.

For his heroic actions, at risk to his own life, two years later Moore was awarded the Navy Cross. He had been promoted to Sergeant by the time of the award.

“...serving with Scout Sniper Platoon, Second Battalion, Eighth Marines, on 14 March 2011 in support of Operation ENDURING FREEDOM. LCpl Moore demonstrated audacity and selfless devotion to duty in the face of a determined enemy when his element came under attack north of Marjah. Two Marines who were outside the structure the team was using for cover immediately became casualties. Insurgents then threw two grenades over the wall into the team's position. Without hesitation and with complete disregard for his own life, LCpl Moore picked up the first grenade and threw it out of the building, where it immediately detonated. He then picked up the second grenade, recognized it had malfunctioned and would not detonate, discarded it, and charged out of the structure to aid the wounded. Though instantly taken under fire by an enemy force one hundred meters away, LCpl Moore stood his ground, returning fire with his M-4 rifle and M-203 grenade launcher. The effects of his fire neutralized the enemy and forced them to abandon their position, buying his team time to regroup and aid their wounded. He then immediately took action to assist in securing a landing zone to extract wounded personnel.”

On a little hill in Pennsylvania, a professor gave an order that saved the Union — and his little brother stood beside him. 🇺🇸

Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain, pictured here, was a Bowdoin College professor of rhetoric who spoke ten languages and had no military training when he talked his way into the Army. By July 2, 1863, he commanded the 20th Maine — and held the extreme left end of the entire Union line on Little Round Top at Gettysburg, with orders to hold "to the last." Among the officers beside him was his younger brother, Lieutenant Thomas Chamberlain.

All afternoon the 20th Maine beat back wave after wave of Alabamians climbing the rocks. Then the ammunition ran out. What Joshua did next is studied in war colleges to this day: he fixed bayonets and ordered a downhill charge — the line swinging like a gate — that swept the stunned Confederates off the hill and, many historians believe, saved the Army of the Potomac. He was wounded so often in that war that newspapers printed his obituary by mistake; Grant chose him to formally receive the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, where Chamberlain ordered his men to salute their defeated enemies as they stacked their arms.

Thomas did not live to see the peace — disease, the silent k*ller of every Civil War camp, claimed him in 1864. Joshua carried his brother's memory through fifty more years: governor, college president, and the old soldier whose name still means Little Round Top.

Can modern forensic breakthroughs finally bring closure to families more than five decades after one of America's most notorious serial killers struck?

Summit County, Utah prosecutors and law enforcement officials have formally linked infamous serial killer Ted Bundy to the unsolved October 1974 murder of 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith through advanced DNA testing.

A 52-Year Cold Case Solved: Melissa Ann Smith disappeared in late October 1974, and her body was later discovered in Summit County by hunters. For decades, her murder remained officially unsolved despite long-standing suspicions regarding Bundy's presence in Utah while attending law school.

The Forensics Breakthrough: Investigators closed the case after connecting genetic evidence preserved from Smith's autopsy to DNA profiles established in the case of Laura Aime—another 17-year-old Utah victim whose murder was definitively tied to Bundy through DNA earlier this year.

Closing the Book on Unsolved Victims: Executed in Florida's electric chair in 1989, Bundy confessed to dozens of killings across Washington, Utah, Colorado, Idaho, and Florida, though several remained unconfirmed. Utah investigators emphasized that every cold case closure helps bring answers to surviving families while bringing permanent resolution to his trail of crimes.

Two brothers of one Wisconsin family — and between them, two of the Civil War's most impossible feats. 🇺🇸

Alonzo Cushing, pictured here, was a 22-year-old artillery lieutenant whose battery stood at the very center of the Union line at Gettysburg — the stone wall called the Angle — on July 3, 1863. As Pickett's Charge rolled toward him, Alonzo was wounded again and again: a shell fragment through the shoulder, another through the body. Ordered to the rear, he refused, had himself held upright beside his last serviceable gun, and was sighting it with his thumb over the vent when a bullet struck him down at his post. The charge broke on the ground he would not leave. In November 2014 — 151 years later — President Barack Obama placed Alonzo Cushing's Medal of Honor where it had always belonged.

His younger brother needed no land battle for his legend. William Barker Cushing of the U.S. Navy, on the night of October 27, 1864, steamed a tiny launch with a spar torpedo up the dark Roanoke River, alone past Confederate guards, and detonated it beneath the ironclad CSS Albemarle — sinking the South's most feared warship and swimming for his life through icy water as it went down.

One brother held the line at the war's turning point. The other sank an ironclad in the dark. America has rarely asked more of one family's sons — and never received more.

The Federal Election Commission (FEC) reporting and filing network has been knocked offline following a suspected cyber incident, severely interrupting the flow of public campaign finance records and 48-hour late-contribution disclosures ahead of national voting.

 Agency databases and electronic submission portals went dark following what cybersecurity officials describe as an external distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) incident and network intrusion attempt, preventing campaigns and PACs from submitting mandated last-minute financial reports.

The outage strikes during the single highest-volume reporting window of the election cycle, blinding oversight groups, reporters, and the public to tens of millions of dollars in final campaign contributions pouring into critical battleground races.

 CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) and federal investigators have stepped in to isolate agency servers, trace potential foreign or domestic threat actors, and restore secure access while issuing emergency paper-filing extensions for affected political committees.

One family. Six months. Four telegrams. 🇺🇸

Alben and Gunda Borgstrom, a farming couple from Thatcher, Utah, sent their sons to war one after another. In 1944, the telegrams began to arrive — and they did not stop.

First came word of Clyde, a Marine on Guadalcanal, lost in March 1944. Then LeRoy, a soldier, gone in the fighting in the summer of 1944. Then Rolon, lost in France. Then Rulon, an airman, missing over Europe and declared d*ad. Four brothers, lost within six months — in the Pacific and in Europe, on the sea of war's every front — while their parents kept the farm and their faith and waited for news of the boys who remained.

What was left of the family's strength, the military itself moved to protect: their fifth serving son, Boyd, was ordered home out of harm's way, released from further combat service so the Borgstrom line would not be extinguished entirely — one of the cases that hardened America's resolve to protect sole surviving sons.

In June 1948, the Army brought the four brothers home together. Thousands gathered in Utah as Clyde, LeRoy, Rolon and Rulon were laid to rest side by side in the Thatcher cemetery — four white markers, one unbearable row, and a nation's debt written in a single family's names.

FORT BENNING, Ga. (USASOC News Service, Dec. 2, 2009) -- A squad leader with the 75th Ranger Regiment was awarded the Silver Star for risking his life to save two fellow Rangers in Afghanistan.

"Any Ranger would have done the same thing," said Staff Sgt. Michael E. Norton of Alpha Company, 3rd Battalion, 75th Rangers. "The Ranger Creed says, 'I will never leave a fallen comrade.' There was no moment of thinking about what to do. I had to get my brothers, and the most important thing in my mind was how hurt they were."

Norton led his squad on an objective, Aug. 4-5, to raid an enemy combatant's headquarters camp in the mountains of northwestern Khowst Province in Afghanistan.

While moving to the objective, Norton and one of his team leaders were alerted to possible enemy combatants along the route and moved forward to assess the situation. As Norton and his team leader were attempting to identify the possible enemy in the valley, a seven—to nine-man enemy element initiated a complex, near ambush on Norton's squad from the high ground with rocket-propelled grenades and small arms fire from a position 25 meters to the squad's front.
"The fire came from our 12 o'clock and then maybe a couple of seconds later from our right and left," Norton said.

Behind the first enemy rocket-propelled grenade team, a medium machine gun on elevated ground to the northwest engaged them with highly effective fire. Two more enemy combatants were on the slope of the valley to the west, engaged the Ranger squad with an AK-47 and rocket-propelled grenades along the long axis of their formation, while another group of enemy fighters were on elevated terrain to the east, raked them with small arms fire from the rear of the Ranger squad formation.

The multiple enemy positions had effectively enveloped Norton's squad from multiple directions at a distance of 25 to 50 meters, leaving Norton and his element pinned to the floor of the valley by the intense and accurate small arms fire.

The valley left no room for maneuver; Norton, his squad and the machine gun team element behind them immediately returned fire, but they were unable to gain fire superiority over the well-established enemy.

After the second rocket-propelled grenades knocked two of his Rangers temporarily unconscious and blasted the rest of his squad with shrapnel and debris and realizing his element could not gain fire superiority, Norton shouted for his squad to break contact.

When Norton realized that two Rangers had not gotten up and were still exposed to the heavy volume of enemy fire from the high ground to the east and west, and with complete disregard for his own safety, Norton turned around and with marked distinction, purposefully charged back into the interlocking fire of the enemy ambush kill zone in order to recover his downed Rangers.

"The example of personal courage that Staff Sergeant Norton showed, to get his men out of the kill zone is a testament to his character," said Maj. Keith Carter, A Company commander. "NCOs such as Staff Sergeant Norton are the reason I wanted to serve in the 75th Ranger Regiment, and it is an honor to lead them."

Without hesitation, Norton dove down into the midst of enemy fire with his unconscious comrades, uncertain of their status.

"There was nothing fancy going on in my head besides hoping they weren't dead," said Norton.

While the rest of the element attempted to suppress the enemy, and lying next to the Rangers, Norton "started shaking and yelling as quietly as I could."

After reviving his Rangers, Norton led them back to cover through the hail of direct fire and rocket-propelled grenade strikes, saving their lives and bringing his entire squad out of the enemy onslaught intact.

"I'm proud of the actions of my squad, because we continued the mission after that," said Norton. "It was just two minutes out of our overall mission."

As his platoon fought off the enemy ambush with direct fire, mortars and close air support, Norton quickly assessed his casualties and reorganized his squad to return to the fight.

Norton continued leading his squad in the follow-on assaults through two more direct fire contacts, killing two enemy combatants.

"We receive a lot of great training here at 3rd Ranger Battalion and I was just acting on instinct," said Norton.

The training conducted by Rangers means everything on the battlefield.

"The goal of the company and battalion is to create the most realistic scenarios possible while minimizing risk," Carter said. We constantly integrate new enemy tactics from overseas into our training so that we are ready in any situation."

The overall assault force killed 20 enemy fighters and destroyed two enemy anti-aircraft guns and several other weapons, explosives, and military supplies on the objective, disrupting a major enemy headquarters and encampment.

Norton joined the Army from his hometown of Pensacola, Fla., June 2004, after graduating from West Highland Christian Academy, and has deployed six times in support of operations Enduring and Iraqi Freedom. He is the son of Jimmy and Deborah Norton of Holly, Mich.

This is the true story behind Saving Private Ryan — and the truth is harder than the film. 🇺🇸

Four brothers from Tonawanda, New York, went to war: Edward, Preston, Robert and Frederick "Fritz" Niland. In one terrible June of 1944, the family's world collapsed. Robert, a paratrooper of the 82nd Airborne, was k*lled on D-Day itself at Neuville-au-Plain. The very next day, June 7, Preston, also a paratrooper, fell near Utah Beach. And from the other side of the world came word that Edward, an airman whose plane had gone down in the Burmese jungle, was missing and presumed d*ad.

That left Fritz, fighting with the 101st Airborne in Normandy. When the Army realized three brothers were gone, it moved fast: the regimental chaplain, Father Francis Sampson, tracked Fritz down and the last Niland son was pulled from the line and sent home to his mother — the real "sole survivor" mission that Steven Spielberg later transformed into Saving Private Ryan.

And then, in 1945, came the telegram no one dared hope for: Edward was alive. Emaciated in a Japanese prison camp, he had survived. Two Niland brothers came home. Two rest side by side today in the American cemetery above Normandy — Preston and Robert, together, under white crosses in Plot B.

Five brothers. One ship. One night that changed America's rules of war forever. 🇺🇸

George, Francis, Joseph, Madison and Albert Sullivan were five Irish-American brothers from Waterloo, Iowa. When their friend Bill Ball was k*lled aboard the USS Arizona at Pearl Harbor, the brothers enlisted together — with one condition the Navy granted: they would serve together. All five were posted to the light cruiser USS Juneau, and their smiling photograph aboard her became one of the famous images of the young war.

On the night of November 13, 1942, in the savage naval battles off Guadalcanal, a Japanese torpedo struck the Juneau's magazine. She disintegrated and sank in less than a minute. Some hundred men survived the sinking and clung to rafts in shark-haunted water — but through a chain of communication failures, no rescue came for days. When help finally arrived, only ten men were pulled out alive. All five Sullivan brothers were gone.

Their mother Alleta received the news with a grace that humbled a nation, and their sister Genevieve joined the Navy's WAVES in their honor. The Navy named a destroyer USS The Sullivans — the only American warship ever named for a family — and the tragedy drove the military to separate siblings and protect sole surviving sons. "We stick together" was the brothers' motto. They did — to the very end.

Before there was a 75th Ranger Regiment, there was one young colonel in Scotland, building America's first Rangers from scratch. 🇺🇸

In the spring of 1942, with America reeling from defeats, Major William Orlando Darby — just 31 years old — was given a mission: create an American unit modeled on the legendary British Commandos. Five hundred volunteers were selected and shipped to Achnacarry, Scotland, where Commando instructors ran them through a course so brutal it used live ammunition. On June 19, 1942, the 1st Ranger Battalion was born — and Darby's men, pictured training here in those early days, were its standard-bearers.

That November, Rangers spearheaded the landings in North Africa, paddling ashore in darkness to silence the guns of Arzew. They fought through Sicily and Italy, at Gela and Salerno and Anzio — and at Cisterna, in January 1944, the 1st and 3rd Ranger Battalions walked into an ambush and were nearly annihilated: of 767 men who went in, only six came back.

Darby refused a safe job in Washington and returned to his men in Italy. On this day, 84 years ago, October 27, 1942, 42-year-old Temporary Lieutenant-Colonel Victor Buller Turner commanded the 2nd Battalion, The Rifle Brigade at a position designated Outpost Snipe during the Second Battle of El Alamein.

His battalion had navigated through enemy minefields overnight to occupy a shallow desert depression near Kidney Ridge, only to find themselves completely isolated at daybreak.

Turner came from a family with a distinct military heritage.

His older brother, Second Lieutenant Alexander Buller Turner, had received a posthumous Victoria Cross in 1915 during the First World War, making them one of only four pairs of brothers in history to win Britain's highest military honor.

He was also related to General Sir Redvers Buller, who earned the Victoria Cross during the Anglo-Zulu War in 1879.

At Outpost Snipe, Turner's force of roughly 300 men with nineteen 6-pounder anti-tank guns faced armored elements of the German 15th and 21st Panzer Divisions and the Italian Ariete Armoured Division.

Axis forces surrounded the position and launched relentless armored counter-attacks with over ninety tanks and self-propelled guns throughout the day.

The desert heat topped 100 degrees Fahrenheit as continuous artillery, mortar, and machine-gun fire rained down into the shallow depression.

Turner moved constantly between his forward anti-tank gun pits on foot to direct fire and keep his men organized under direct shellfire.

Targeting German Panzer III and IV tanks, the gun crews held their fire until enemy armor closed within 100 yards to ensure maximum penetration.

As casualties mounted, several 6-pounder anti-tank guns were left unmanned or severely shorthanded.

When one vital gun pit was stripped of its crew except for an officer and a sergeant, Turner ran across open, bullet-swept ground to join them.

He immediately stepped into the role of loader, hauling heavy 6-pounder solid-shot shells and jamming them into the breech.

Exposed from the waist up to direct machine-gun and tank cannon fire, Turner loaded round after round as the crew engaged German armor at point-blank range.

Together, this single gun crew destroyed five German tanks at a distance of less than 50 yards before the attack stalled.

While carrying ammunition shells to keep the gun operational, a high-explosive shell burst nearby, spraying shrapnel into Turner's head.

The fragment inflicted a severe scalp wound that bled heavily down his face and neck.

Turner refused medical evacuation, brushed off aid, and remained on his feet at the forward perimeter to direct the remaining guns.

By the time the battle ended, Turner's battalion had destroyed or disabled 37 enemy tanks and self-propelled guns, shattering the Axis armored counter-offensive.

King George VI presented Turner with the Victoria Cross at Buckingham Palace on July 27, 1943.

After the war, Turner remained in the British Army and retired with the rank of Lieutenant-Colonel.

He was later appointed to the Royal Household as a Yeoman of the Guard in 1950.

In 1966, he was made a Commander of the Royal Victorian Order, and in 1967 he became Lieutenant of the Queen's Bodyguard of the Yeomen of the Guard.

Victor Buller Turner died on August 7, 1972, at the age of 72 in Ditchingham, Norfolk, and his Victoria Cross is currently displayed at the Royal Green Jackets Museum in Winchester.

They marched a thousand miles through jungle, fought an empire, and dissolved almost to the last man. 🇺🇸

In February 1944, some 3,000 American volunteers — jungle fighters, muleskinners, and men who spoke languages of the Pacific — slipped behind Japanese lines in Burma. Officially they were the 5307th Composite Unit. History knows them by their commander, Brigadier General Frank Merrill: Merrill's Marauders.

With only what they and their mules could carry, they marched farther than any American unit of the war — some 750 to 1,000 miles of mountain and jungle — and fought five major battles and dozens of skirmishes, cutting the supply lines of an army that outnumbered them many times over. Their true enemies were as much malaria, dysentery, and scrub typhus as the Japanese: men fought with fevers of 104 degrees, and the wounded who could walk were sent back to the line.

When the airfield at Myitkyina finally fell in August 1944, of the nearly 3,000 who had marched in, only about 200 remained fit for duty. Every Marauder received the Bronze Star, and in 2020 Congress awarded the unit its Gold Medal. Their legacy marches on today in the 75th Ranger Regiment, which carries the Marauders' lineage — and their impossible standard.

Their tanks were rubber. Their guns were dummies. And they saved thousands of lives. Meet the Ghost Army. 🇺🇸

In the summer of 1944, a strange unit landed in France: the 23rd Headquarters Special Troops — 1,100 men recruited not for their shooting, but for their sketchbooks. They were art students, designers, actors, architects and sound engineers, and their mission was pure deception: to impersonate entire American divisions — 30,000 men — with inflatable tanks, dummy aircraft, giant speakers blasting recorded sounds of armies on the move, and fake radio traffic.

Again and again, the Ghost Army set up its theater near the front while the real divisions slipped away to attack somewhere else. German reconnaissance saw the "tanks," heard the "army," and aimed at ghosts. Historians credit the unit with saving between 15,000 and 30,000 American lives — and then the whole story was classified for half a century. The artists never got their parade.

That finally changed on March 21, 2024, when the surviving Ghost Army veterans — most near a hundred years old — received the Congressional Gold Medal in Washington. One of their inflatable Sherman tanks, like the one pictured here, survives today in a museum: a balloon that helped win a war.

Remembering the legendary courage, fierce defiance, and ultimate sacrifice of Commander Ernest E. Evans and the crew of the USS Johnston (DD-557) during the Battle off Samar.

Outgunned by enemy battleships whose individual gun turrets weighed more than the entire Johnston, the destroyer launched a fierce torpedo attack that crippled a heavy cruiser, dodging thousands of tons of incoming armor-piercing shells. Though battered to a standstill, stripped of power, and severely damaged with half her crew wounded or killed, the Johnston kept firing until her guns jammed, with Commander Evans manually operating a gun mount himself.

ON THIS DAY — October 31, 1941: America loses its first warship of World War II — before the war even begins. 🇺🇸

In the autumn of 1941, the United States was officially at peace — but in the North Atlantic, its Navy was already fighting. American destroyers escorted convoys of supplies to Britain through waters prowled by German U-boats, and everyone knew the shooting war at sea had quietly started.

In the early hours of October 31, 1941, the destroyer USS Reuben James (DD-245), an aging four-stack ship escorting convoy HX-156, moved to shield the merchant ships from a suspected submarine. The U-552 fired first. A torpedo struck the Reuben James at her forward magazine, and the little destroyer broke in two and sank in under five minutes. Of her crew, 115 men were lost; only 44 survived — not one officer among them.

The Reuben James was the first United States Navy warship sunk in the Second World War — five weeks before Pearl Harbor — and her loss shook the nation so deeply it became a famous folk song by Woody Guthrie. On this day in 1941, 115 American sailors became the first of more than 400,000 who would not come home from that war.

ON THIS DAY — October 30, 1961: the biggest explosion in human history. 🇺🇸

At the height of the Cold War, the Soviet Union built a bomb so large it was almost a stunt: the Tsar Bomba, a hydrogen bomb designed for 100 megatons — more than 3,000 times the power of the bomb that destroyed Hiroshima — and deliberately halved to about 50 megatons so its own bomber might survive dropping it.

On October 30, 1961, over the frozen test range at Novaya Zemlya in the Arctic, a Tu-95 bomber released it by parachute and dove away at full throttle. The fireball rose miles into the sky and was seen more than 600 miles away. Windows shattered in Finland and Norway. The shockwave circled the entire Earth three times, and the mushroom cloud punched into the stratosphere.

The blast convinced the world it had seen the edge of madness: within two years, the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union signed the treaty banning atmospheric nuclear tests. The Tsar Bomba was never a practical weapon. It was a message — and on this day in 1961, the whole planet heard it.

ON THIS DAY — October 29, 1969: "LO." The first words of the internet. 🇺🇸

The internet was born as a military project. The Pentagon's Advanced Research Projects Agency — ARPA — wanted its research computers across America to talk to each other, so it built a network called ARPANET, with special router machines called Interface Message Processors.

On the night of October 29, 1969, a student programmer at UCLA named Charley Kline sat at a terminal and attempted the first host-to-host login to a computer at Stanford Research Institute, 350 miles away. He typed L — it arrived. He typed O — it arrived. He typed G — and the system crashed. The first message ever sent across what became the internet was "LO," as in "lo and behold."

Within a few years, this Cold War experiment was carrying the military's and universities' data. Within a generation, it had become the internet — the network beneath the phone in your pocket began with two letters, a crash, and a Pentagon idea on this day in 1969.

ON THIS DAY — October 28, 1942: the impossible road is finished. 🇺🇸

When Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Alaska was almost unreachable — no road connected it to the rest of America, and Japanese forces soon occupied Aleutian islands. The Army's answer sounded insane: carve a 1,500-mile military highway through unmapped Canadian wilderness, muskeg, mountains and permafrost, before winter.

More than ten thousand soldiers did it — and a third of them were African American engineer regiments, men the Army had largely sidelined to labor duty, working in the worst conditions with the worst equipment, in cold that froze machinery and men alike. They felled forests, bridged wild rivers like the Peace, and laid road at a pace no one believed possible.

On October 28, 1942 — just eight months after the first bulldozer rolled — the Alaska Highway was completed, and soldiers from north and south met and shook hands on the finished road. It still carries travelers today, a monument built by hands America almost refused to use.

Benjamin O. On May 2, 1968, Captain James E. Livingston led Echo Company, 2nd Battalion, 4th Marines, in an assault on the fortified village of Dai Do in Vietnam's Quang Tri Province — one of the fiercest fights of the war.

Livingston charged at the head of his men from bunker to bunker. Wounded in the leg, he refused medical aid and kept attacking. When a sister company was pinned down and surrounded, he led a rescue force across open ground under murderous fire, was wounded a second and then a third time — and still refused evacuation until he had personally made sure every one of his wounded Marines was carried out first. Only then did he allow himself to be taken to the rear, collapsing from loss of blood.

President Richard Nixon presented him the Medal of Honor on May 14, 1970. James Livingston served more than thirty years, retiring as a Major General — and the Marines of Dai Do never forgot the captain who would not leave the field while a single one of his men remained on it.

After nearly 28 years of service in the U.S. Army, Brigadier General Terence John Hildner was serving in Afghanistan when his life ended unexpectedly. On February 3, 2012, the 49-year-old commander of the 13th Sustainment Command (Expeditionary) was found deceased in his quarters in Kabul. Officials said he appeared to have died of natural causes, not in combat. At the time, he was the highest-ranking American service member reported to have died during the Afghanistan War.

Born in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1962, Hildner grew up in a military family, moving between places including Japan, Italy, and Colorado. He graduated from the University of Notre Dame in 1984 and began his Army career as a commissioned officer.

His early assignments included service with the 3rd Armored Cavalry Regiment at Fort Bliss and the 2nd Armored Cavalry Regiment in West Germany. He commanded a cavalry troop and took part in the final American patrol along the East-West German border before reunification.

When Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, Hildner and his troop deployed with the U.S. VII Corps during Operation Desert Storm. He later moved into Army logistics, taking on the vital work of making sure troops had the supplies, equipment, and support needed to carry out their missions.

In 2003, he led the Special Troops Battalion of the 13th Corps Support Command at Fort Hood. The unit deployed to Iraq, supporting U.S. forces near Joint Base Balad and Abu Ghraib, and later assisted with relief operations after Hurricane Katrina. From 2007 to 2009, he commanded the 23rd Quartermaster Brigade at Fort Lee, which trained more than 20,000 soldiers each year.

In 2010, Hildner assumed command of the 13th Sustainment Command (Expeditionary). The following year, he deployed to Afghanistan as deputy commander for support operations with NATO Training Mission–Afghanistan. His work included helping Afghan leaders build systems to supply and maintain their security forces.

His death in Kabul brought profound grief to his family and the soldiers who served with him. His father, Robert, told The Washington Post that he believed Terence may have suffered a heart attack; this was a family member’s belief, not a confirmed medical finding. Army accounts described the death as due to natural causes. No enemy attack or combat injury was reported.

Hildner was survived by his wife, Cindy, their four children, his parents, and his siblings. His father remembered him for his humor, determination, and analytical mind. On February 29, 2012, he was laid to rest with military honors at Arlington National Cemetery.

His decorations included the Legion of Merit, two Bronze Star Medals, the Defense Meritorious Service Medal, and the Combat Action Badge—honors earned over a career that spanned multiple conflicts and senior leadership roles.

His story is a reminder that service members can be lost overseas not only in combat, but also to illness and other non-combat circumstances. Brigadier General Terence John Hildner was a husband, father, son, and dedicated Army officer whose service ended far from home.

Rest peacefully, General Hildner. Your commitment to your soldiers and family will not be forgotten.

Marcus Luttrell (born November 7, 1975) is a former United States Navy SEAL who received the Navy Cross and Purple Heart for his actions in June 2005 facing Taliban fighters during Operation Red Wings. Luttrell was a Hospital Corpsman First Class by the end of his eight-year career in the United States Navy.

He was deployed to Afghanistan in 2005 with SEAL Team Ten as part of SEAL Delivery Vehicle Team One (SDV-1).[4] While in Afghanistan, he was involved in Operation Red Wings, during which the four-man Special Reconnaissance element with SDV-1 was discovered by local herdsmen, subsequently ambushed, and all killed except for Luttrell. Luttrell was awarded the Navy Cross for his actions during the operation. The team knew the local herdsmen might reveal their whereabouts to Taliban fighters but because they were not armed combatants, they were allowed to leave despite the risk to themselves and their mission.

The ambush during Operation Red Wings was intense. The four SEALs were attacked from three sides, and included fire from PK machine guns, AK-47s, RPG-7s, and 82mm mortars. The attack forced the SEALs into the northeast gulch of the Shuryek Valley side of Sawtalo Sar. The SEALs made a number of attempts to contact their combat operations center with a PRC-148 MBITR (Multi Band Inter/Intra Team Radio) and then with an Iridium Satellite Phone. They could not establish consistent communication, however, other than for a period long enough to indicate that they were under attack. Three of the four team members were killed, and Luttrell, being the only survivor, was left unconscious with a number of fractures, a broken back, and numerous shrapnel wounds. Members of SEAL Team 10 attempted a rescue during the firefight but their helicopter was shot down and all aboard were killed. Luttrell regained consciousness and evaded the pursuing enemy with the help of local Pashtun villagers, who eventually sent an emissary to the nearest U.S. base to secure his safe rescue and ultimately save his life. After recovering from his injuries, he returned to active duty and deployed to Ramadi during Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2006 as part of SEAL Team Five. He later had his knees blown out and fractured his spine again. This ultimately led to his discharge.

The families told the soldiers the Taliban made the other people leave the village, but that having nowhere to go. they stayed. “What was alarming,” Ward said later, “was the buildings had locks and barricaded doors, which was a clear indication that the village wasn't abandoned, but had been turned into a defendable position.”

All three quickly figured it was only a matter of time before the firefight would begin.
The teams were quickly engaged by 300 Taliban fighters. According to Army documents, after an hour of fighting, two vehicles were pulled to the rear of the fight after being disabled. This left the ground forces commander to the front of the coalition lines and in jeopardy of being overrun. At this point, Ward, the team leader for 745, radioed to the ground forces commander, who was pinned down in a vulnerable building, that his was on its way. Ward later said he and Alcazar went because they were the closest truck and the others were busy providing cover. Unfortunately, the team's vehicle crashed into an enemy fighting position and became immobile, knocking Ward and Alcazar momentarily unconscious.
After they regained consciousness, Alcazar took to reloading ammunition belts, enabling Kimmey, the gunner, to continue to engage enemy forces. Ward exited the vehicle and directed his team to dismount and move to cover. Kimmey remained in the turret, providing cover for the team and allowing them to reach the ground forces commander. He stayed even though he knew the enemy was setting up mortar positions to destroy the truck he was firing from.

Kimmey was able to keep the Taliban from overrunning the soldiers with the .50-caliber gun. In the process, he was drawing a majority of the enemy fire. Ward reported the enemy was about 50 to 100 meters away at this point.

Team 745 moved to the ground commander's position and helped in the recovery of the commander and the casualties. All of this was done, while under “continual, accurate and effective” enemy fire.

Since the team's 745's vehicle was immobile, it was stripped of all sensitive equipment, and its gun was dismantled to prevent the enemy from gaining off of the team's loss. Once team 745 sterilized their truck, they had no choice but to run beside the Special Forces vehicle, using it as cover, until they reached safety, because there was no room for them on the truck. All three of them ran alongside the truck until they reached a checkpoint and mounted up into another vehicle for the ride back to Firebase Cobra.

During the civil affairs award ceremony, all three were honored for their heroic acts. Maj. Gen. John F. Mulholland, said, “The words can't do justice, nor can the medal on your chest convey what they went up against.”

On this day, 84 years ago, October 25, 1942, 40-year-old Private Percival Eric Gratwick faced heavy enemy fire during the Second Battle of El Alamein in Egypt.

Before enlisting, Gratwick worked as a gold prospector and station hand in the remote Pilbara region of Western Australia.

He served in the 2/48th Infantry Battalion, a unit that became Australia's most decorated battalion of World War II, earning four Victoria Crosses in total.

On the night of October 25, his company launched an attack on Trig 29 along Miteiriya Ridge.

Intense machine-gun and mortar fire from German and Italian positions pinned down Gratwick's platoon in open terrain.

Enfilade fire quickly killed the platoon commander, the platoon sergeant, and most of the men, leaving only seven survivors.

Recognizing that remaining pinned down meant total destruction, Gratwick acted on his own initiative.

He collected hand grenades, stood up into the line of fire, and charged the nearest enemy mortar position alone.

He reached the trench, threw his grenades, and killed the entire mortar crew.

With that position destroyed, Gratwick spotted a second enemy machine-gun post hurling heavy fire at his advancing company.

Armed only with his rifle and fixed bayonet, he immediately ran across open ground toward the machine gun.

He closed the distance under direct fire, charging into close-quarters combat and inflicting casualties on the defenders.

As he reached striking distance of the gun, a burst of machine-gun fire struck Gratwick, killing him instantly.

His solo attack destroyed key strongpoints and rattled the surviving enemy defenders.

Inspired by his charge, the rest of the company advanced, cleared the remaining enemy positions, and captured the final objective.

Gratwick had celebrated his 40th birthday just six days before giving his life in the assault.

On January 28, 1943, the British Crown posthumously awarded Private Percival Eric Gratwick the Victoria Cross.

He was buried at the El Alamein War Cemetery in Egypt at Plot XXII, Row A, Grave 6.

His mother accepted the Victoria Cross on his behalf, and the medal is now displayed at the Army Museum of Western Australia in Fremantle.

Ramadi, 2006. The most dangerous city on Earth — and this SEAL officer led from the front of it. 🇺🇸

Leif Babin served as a Navy SEAL officer with SEAL Team Three, deploying to Ramadi, Iraq, in 2006 as a platoon commander in Task Unit Bruiser — the most decorated special operations unit of the Iraq War. Under his task unit commander, Jocko Willink, Babin led his platoon through relentless urban combat in a city the enemy was determined to hold.

Babin was awarded the Silver Star, a Bronze Star and the Purple Heart for his service in that fight, where his platoon helped turn the tide in Anbar Province alongside American soldiers, Marines and brave Iraqi forces.

But his most famous battle began after the war. In 2015, Babin and Willink published "Extreme Ownership," the leadership book built entirely on the hard lessons of Ramadi — that there are no bad teams, only bad leaders, and that a leader owns everything in his world. The book became a phenomenon read in boardrooms, locker rooms and military units around the globe.

Through their company Echelon Front, Babin still teaches the same principle he proved in combat: leadership is everything.

The 23rd and 24th of June 2006 would be a crucible of leadership and heroism for an already battle-tested and decorated captain in the U.S. Army's Special Forces. Captain Sheffield F. Ford III was in charge of some 16 Americans and 46 Afghan Army soldiers during "Operation Kaika" in the Panjawi District of Afghanistan's Kandahar province.

In the bleak farmland, crisscrossed by ditches and barren expanses, Ford led his unit to "re-establish order" in the contested region, entering a Spartan Afghan village on the 23rd. The dilapidated buildings and mud huts were hiding a Taliban force of unknown strength with one thought on their minds: killing Americans and the Afghan soldiers working to take back their country. In their hastily prepared patrol base, Ford organized a perimeter as night enveloped the isolated Special Forces team and their Afghan allies.

As darkness fell, "all hell [broke] loose." From three directions, rifle, machine gun, and rocket-propelled grenade fire landed and exploded on their position. One of Ford's squad mates later said they had "not seen this disciplined execution of infantry tactics" by the Taliban. Ford dug his men in to repel the assault.

Moving from position to position, he alternated between barking orders, firing at the enemy, and rallying the Afghan soldiers with him. As the night crept on, the remaining Taliban fighters withdrew and Ford took stock of the situation.

Early the next day, he ordered some of his Special Forces operators to lead a team of Afghans into the suspected Taliban hideout. As the unit engaged the hostiles, it was divided in two when some 200 Taliban fighters poured out, separating the American attackers and surrounding the make-shift patrol base.

Over the radio, Ford was connected with one of the translators who had been leading the mission on the Taliban position. The translator saw two Americans were fighting despite being severely wounded and feared capture at any minute. Knowing the ramifications of being taken alive by the Taliban, the translator told Ford he would, if ordered, end the suffering of the troops and his own life rather than be captured. Ford responded, "We've got people coming." Ford organized and launched an effective rescue to recover the translator and wounded troops, even if they were mortally wounded. He would not allow American or Afghan alike to be taken in any condition by the Taliban.

The adversaries fought so close to one another that the terrorists screamed to the Afghan soldiers that, "we can forgive you; just put your weapons down and walk away. We want the Americans alive." The months of training and the ties formed between the Americans and the Afghans were put to the test. Seeing the example of Ford running to each of the beleaguered fighters in the face of constant fire, and remembering all they had endured alongside their American trainers, the Afghan soldiers responded to the Taliban's offer with well-aimed shots and an unbreakable defense.

Exemplifying the U.S. Special Forces motto, De Opresso Liber (to liberate the oppressed), Ford inspired his Afghan troops to stand up to the Taliban fighters and bring them down. He led an evacuation of all the men under his command, wounded included, out of the village under the cover of Apache attack choppers to ensure all would be safe while sealing the fate of the insurgents. Ford successfully extricated his men, and the unit had more than 120 confirmed kills. Just as the Americans and Afghans had trained together, they sacrificed together; two American and three Afghan soldiers would not leave the battlefield alive. For his accomplishments in the face of such an overpowering force, Ford was awarded the Silver Star, the nation's third highest military award.

He led real SEAL missions — then he played himself in the film, so America could finally see the real thing. 🇺🇸

Commander Rorke Denver spent his career the way SEALs prefer it: quietly. As an officer with SEAL Team Three, he led platoons on combat deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan, earning the Bronze Star with Valor for his leadership under fire.

Then, in a first for the U.S. military, Denver and his fellow active-duty SEALs starred as themselves in the 2012 film "Act of Valor." No actors pretending — the men on screen jumping from planes, clearing rooms and kicking in doors were the real warriors, performing live-fire tactics. Denver's face became, for millions of Americans, the face of the modern SEAL.

After hanging up his uniform, he put his story on paper in his book "Damn Few: Making the Modern SEAL Warrior," an honest look at what it takes to earn the Trident and carry its burden.

His philosophy is simple and famous among the Teams: calm is contagious — and so is panic. A leader's job is to bring the calm.
